topics.title: Design Snake & Ladder
topics.markdown:
## Problem

Design Snake & Ladder: N players take turns rolling dice and move along a board of 100 cells; snakes send you down, ladders send you up, and the first to reach 100 wins. Interviewers use it to test a **game-engine abstraction**: clean entities, configurable rules and **Strategy** for dice and rule variations.

## Requirements

**Functional**
- Configurable board size, snakes and ladders (validated: no cycles, nothing starting at the end cell).
- 2+ players in a turn queue. One or more dice.
- Rule variants: exact roll needed to finish, extra turn on a 6, three 6s forfeits the turn.
- Report each move and the winner. Optionally continue to rank all players.

**Non-functional**
- Deterministic and testable: dice and randomness are injectable (seeded).
- Rule variants are configurable without changing the game loop.
- The board is validated once at setup, not during play.

## 1. Scope and chosen solution

I choose a 100-square board, six-sided dice, exact landing to win, one jump per landing and first winner ends the game. No bonus turn for six in this ruleset. The board validates jump endpoints and direction; snakes descend and ladders ascend.

## 2. Turn execution

```text
playTurn(playerId):
  verify active game and expected player
  roll injected dice, require 1..6
  candidate = position + roll
  if candidate > 100: final = old position
  else: final = jumpMap.getOrDefault(candidate,candidate)
  commit roll, old/final position and winner or next player
```

At 14 with roll 3 and ladder 17→38, final position is 38. At 97 with roll 5, it stays 97. One-jump resolution cannot loop even if arbitrary map data contains a cycle; I still reject invalid self-jumps and endpoints at construction. A chained-jump extension uses a visited set and rejects cycles. Concurrent turn calls serialize at Game, preventing two dice rolls for the same accepted turn/version. Expected dice value 3.5 does not equal net progress because jumps and overshoots alter movement.

## 3. Final design diagram

[![Design Snake & Ladder: Game uses Board; Game rotates Player; Game rolls through Dice; Game advances with TurnPolicy; Board resolves jumps JumpResolver; Game records MoveHistory](designs/lld-17.svg)](designs/lld-17.svg)

The **board** stores snakes and ladders, the **dice source** produces a roll, and the **game** owns turn order and player positions. Randomness is an input boundary, so tests should supply predetermined rolls rather than hope the right number appears.

## 4. Critical operation: worked execution

![The game applies movement policy before resolving a jump.](lessons/lld-17-flow.svg)

*The game applies movement policy before resolving a jump.*

![Validate jump chains or restrict the board to one jump per landing.](lessons/lld-17-failure.svg)

*Validate jump chains or restrict the board to one jump per landing.*

### Selected algorithm

```java
// Rule sketch: exact landing; an overshoot leaves the position unchanged.
int advance(int current, int roll, int lastSquare) {
    if (roll < 1 || roll > 6) throw new IllegalArgumentException();
    int target = current + roll;
    return target > lastSquare ? current : target;
}
```

For a board with six-sided dice, the expected single roll is `(1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 3.5`. That is not the expected net movement once snakes, ladders and overshoot rules apply. Avoid replacing the actual board process with this average when explaining game duration.

## 5. Detailed decisions, algorithms and failure behaviour

### Key abstractions

| Type | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `Game` | Turn loop, winner detection |
| `Board` | size, `Map<Integer, Integer> jumps` (start → end) |
| `Jump` (or `Snake`/`Ladder` subtypes) | start, end; a snake has end < start |
| `Player` | name, position |
| `Dice` (Strategy) | `StandardDice(count)`, `CrookedDice` (only even numbers), `FixedDice` for tests |
| `RuleSet` | `ExactFinishRule`, `ExtraTurnOnSix`, `ThreeSixesForfeit` |
| `BoardFactory` | Builds a board from config and validates it |

```java
int move(Player p, int roll) {
    int target = p.position() + roll;
    if (target > board.size()) return p.position();     // exact-finish rule
    return board.jumps().getOrDefault(target, target);   // O(1) snake/ladder
}
```

### Design decisions & trade-offs

**1. Snakes and ladders are the same thing.** Both are a jump from `start` to `end`. One `Map<Integer, Integer>` handles both in O(1). Separate classes add nothing except display labels. This is a nice "avoid needless inheritance" point.

**2. Dice as a Strategy.** It makes the game testable: inject `FixedDice(4, 2, 6)` to script a game. Variants (two dice, crooked dice) don't touch `Game`.

**3. Rules as composable objects.** Rule toggles change between house variants. A list of `Rule` objects consulted in order (`afterRoll`, `canFinish`, `grantsExtraTurn`) keeps the turn loop stable.

**4. Turn order.** Use a `Deque<Player>`: poll, play, offer back (unless they finished or forfeit). With an extra-turn rule, re-offer to the front.

**5. Board validation.** Reject jumps that start at 1 or 100, jumps that land on another jump's start (chains), and two jumps from the same cell. Fail at construction, not mid-game.

### Ownership, boundaries and invariants

**Central design question:** Make game rules explicit, especially overshoot and whether special squares chain.

Board maps starting squares to Jump targets; Game owns Players and current turn. Dice is an injected source of bounded values. MovePolicy handles exact-finish rules; TurnPolicy handles extra turns. Randomness is a dependency so tests can be deterministic.

**Correctness rule:** Player positions stay within board bounds, every jump target is valid, and terminal games stop accepting moves. A malformed jump cycle cannot cause an infinite turn.

```text
game(id,board_size,current_player,version); player(id,position); jump(from_square,to_square); turn(id,roll,result)
```

### End-to-end execution trace

Verify current player; obtain a dice value from the configured dice; compute tentative square; apply overshoot policy; resolve the allowed snake/ladder behavior with a visited set if chaining is supported; commit the final position; declare victory or advance turn.

### Concurrency and recovery walkthrough

Two roll commands for the same turn use different random values. A turn request ID and aggregate version prevent both from advancing the game; persist the chosen roll before returning success.

### Policy choices and extension seams

A map from square to destination is sufficient for snakes and ladders. Subclasses for every snake add little value. Strategy becomes useful for house rules, number of dice or finish behavior.

### Edge cases that change the design

Reject jumps from or to invalid squares, duplicate jump origins and forbidden start/end cells. Decide whether landing on a ladder leads to another jump. Do not quietly hard-code a popular house rule as the only valid ruleset.

**Topic-specific cases:** Deterministic dice; overshoot; exact finish; cycle detection; extra-turn rule; duplicate roll command; board configuration validation.

### Further reading

- [Java 21 concurrency contracts](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/package-summary.html) — synchronization and executor semantics.
- [PostgreSQL transaction isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html) — database guarantees differ from process locks.

### Work through extension seams

Represent jumps as data `start -> end`; validate endpoints inside the board and forbid a zero-length jump. If the chosen rules allow at most one jump per turn, document that instead of accidentally chaining jumps because the implementation uses recursion.

Rules such as “roll six again” and “three sixes lose the turn” belong in a turn policy with an explicit roll history. They do not belong in the physical dice implementation. A replay log should store actual rolls and committed moves so results remain reproducible even if a random generator changes.

## 6. Interviewer follow-ups

**How do you test a ladder landing?** Inject a roll that reaches its starting square and assert the final destination.

**Should a winner keep receiving turns?** No. Define whether the game ends at first victory or ranks all players, then enforce that terminal policy.

## 7. Closing answer

I make board jumps data and inject dice results, while Game owns deterministic turn transitions. Exact-landing and one-jump-per-landing are explicit policies. A move log records actual rolls, so tests and replay do not depend on randomness.

topics.title: Metrics / Time-Series System
topics.markdown:
## Problem

Design a metrics and monitoring system like Prometheus at scale, Datadog metrics or M3. Every service reports numbers – requests per second, error rate, p99 latency, CPU – every 10 seconds. Dashboards draw them as graphs, and an alert pages the on-call engineer when, for example, the checkout error rate stays above 2% for 5 minutes.

Unlike logs, metrics are small numbers, but there are millions of separate series, and queries aggregate over many of them at once.

## Requirements

- Collect numeric metrics with labels (service, region, endpoint) from thousands of services.
- Store them as time series; query and aggregate over time ranges for dashboards.
- Evaluate alert rules continuously and notify the on-call engineer.
- Keep raw data for 15 days and downsampled data for a year.
- Stay up during incidents – that is when people need it most.

## Step 1: Clarify the requirements

> **💡 Tip**
> The key number in metrics is not bytes but **active series** – each unique combination of metric name and labels.

**Candidate:** How many services and series?

**Interviewer:** 5,000 services; about 50 million active series.

**Candidate:** How often are values collected?

**Interviewer:** Every 10 seconds.

**Candidate:** Push or pull?

**Interviewer:** Your choice – explain it.

**Candidate:** How fast must alerts fire?

**Interviewer:** Within a minute of the condition being true.

**Candidate:** How long do we keep data?

**Interviewer:** 15 days at full resolution, a year at lower resolution.

**Functional requirements**

1. Collect counters, gauges and histograms with labels.
2. Query with aggregation (sum, rate, percentiles) over time ranges.
3. Alert rules with notifications.

**Non-functional requirements**

1. Ingest 5 million samples per second.
2. Dashboard queries in under a second for common ranges.
3. Alerting keeps working even if dashboards are slow.

## Step 2: Estimate the scale

> **💡 Tip**
> Time-series compression is remarkable: a sample costs about 1–2 bytes, not 16.

```text
Active series        = 50 million
Samples per second   = 50M / 10 s        = 5 million per second
Raw size per sample  = 8-byte timestamp + 8-byte value = 16 bytes
Compressed           ≈ 1.5 bytes (Gorilla-style delta encoding)
Per day              = 5M × 86,400 × 1.5 B ≈ 650 GB/day
15 days              ≈ 10 TB (plus replicas)
```

What it means: storage is fine thanks to compression. The real limits are active series in memory and query fan-out.

## Step 3: Define the API

```text
# Exposed by each service at /metrics (Prometheus text format)
http_requests_total{service="checkout",endpoint="/pay",status="500"} 1832
http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{service="checkout",le="0.5"} 98211
```

```http
GET /api/v1/query_range?query=sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout",status=~"5.."}[5m]))
                         / sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout"}[5m]))
                        &start=…&end=…&step=30s
```

Alert rule:

```yaml
- alert: CheckoutErrorRateHigh
  expr: checkout_error_ratio > 0.02
  for: 5m
  labels: { severity: page }
```

> **🎯 In the interview**
> Explain counter + `rate()`: services expose a counter that only goes up; the query takes its per-second rate over a window. Restarts reset counters, and `rate()` handles that.

## Step 4: Define the data model

A **series** is a metric name plus a set of labels. It has an ID and a list of (timestamp, value) samples.

| Store | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| Series index | label → series IDs (an inverted index, like search) |
| Head block (memory) | the last ~2 hours of samples, plus a write-ahead log on disk |
| Blocks | immutable 2-hour chunks of compressed samples, later merged into larger blocks |
| Long-term store | downsampled (5-minute, 1-hour) blocks in object storage |

> **⚖️ Design choice**
> A purpose-built time-series database (Prometheus/Thanos, M3, VictoriaMetrics), not a general SQL table. Append-only, time-ordered, compressed blocks are 10× cheaper and much faster.

## Step 5: Draw the high-level design

[![High-level design: instrumented services expose metrics to collectors; ingest applies label and series limits and writes time-series blocks; the query engine reads blocks for dashboards; an alert evaluator runs rules on a schedule; old blocks are downsampled into long-term rollups.](designs/hld-17.svg)](designs/hld-17.svg)

**Collect and store**

1. Each service exposes `/metrics`. A collector **scrapes** it every 10 seconds (pull).
2. Ingest checks limits (max series per service), then appends samples to the head block of the right shard, chosen by hashing the series.
3. Every 2 hours the head block is compressed and flushed; blocks are uploaded to object storage.

**Query and alert**

1. A dashboard query is split by time range and shard; each shard returns partial aggregates; the query engine merges them.
2. The alert evaluator runs every rule every 30 seconds. If a rule stays true for its `for:` duration, it sends the alert to the **alert manager**, which groups, silences and routes it to Slack or PagerDuty.

![Animation: the checkout error ratio rises above 2 percent; the alert enters pending; it stays above the threshold for five minutes and becomes firing; the alert manager groups it and pages the on-call engineer; the ratio falls and the alert resolves.](learning-figures/hld-17-alert.gif)

## Step 6: Go deep

### Push or pull?

**Option 1: Pull (scrape), like Prometheus.**

- Good: the monitoring system controls the rate; a failed scrape itself tells you the target is down.
- Problem: needs service discovery to know what to scrape; awkward for short-lived jobs.

**Option 2: Push, like StatsD or OpenTelemetry exporters.**

- Good: works for short jobs and through firewalls.
- Problem: a misbehaving client can flood you; you need quotas.

> **⚖️ Design choice**
> Pull for long-running services, push (through a gateway with quotas) for batch jobs and serverless functions. Many real systems support both.

### Cardinality: the number one danger

Every unique label combination is a new series held in memory. Adding a label like `userId` turns one series into 10 million.

```text
http_requests_total{service, endpoint, status}       → 5,000 × 20 × 5   = 500,000 series
… plus userId (10M users)                             → 5 trillion series  ✗
```

> **⚠️ Common mistake**
> Putting unbounded values (user IDs, order IDs, full URLs) in labels. Use them in logs or traces; keep labels to small, fixed sets.

[![Cardinality limits: a new series is checked against per-service and per-metric limits; known label values pass; a label with unbounded values such as user IDs is rejected or dropped before it can exhaust memory.](learning-figures/hld-17-cardinality.svg)](learning-figures/hld-17-cardinality.svg)

### Storing samples compactly

Samples arrive in time order, and consecutive values are similar. Store the difference between timestamps (usually exactly 10 s, so it compresses to almost nothing) and XOR consecutive values (Facebook's Gorilla technique). That is how 16 bytes become about 1.5.

### Downsampling for long ranges

A one-year graph does not need 10-second points. A background job turns old raw data into 5-minute and 1-hour summaries (min, max, sum, count) stored in object storage. Year-long queries read the summaries.

### Keep alerting independent

Run alert evaluation close to the data with its own resources, and have a "watchdog" alert that always fires – if the on-call system stops hearing it, the monitoring itself is broken.

## Step 7: Find bottlenecks and failure points

| What fails | What happens | How we handle it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A team adds a `userId` label | Memory explodes | Per-service series limits; reject new series over the limit |
| An ingest shard crashes | Recent samples lost | Write-ahead log; two replicas per shard |
| A huge dashboard query | Slows everything | Query limits, timeouts, cached results, downsampled data |
| Monitoring is down during an incident | Flying blind | Separate, small meta-monitoring and a watchdog alert |
| An alert flaps on and off | Pager fatigue | `for:` duration, grouping and silences |

## Putting it together

- **Collect:** scrape `/metrics` (or push with quotas) → limit series → append to sharded head blocks.
- **Store:** compressed 2-hour blocks → object storage → downsampled rollups.
- **Use:** merged queries for dashboards; rules with `for:` → alert manager → on-call.

## Interviewer follow-ups

**How do you compute p99 latency across 100 servers?** Each server exposes a histogram (counts per latency bucket). Sum the buckets across servers, then estimate the percentile. You cannot average per-server p99s.

**How is this different from logging?** Metrics are pre-aggregated numbers – cheap, fast, good for alerts and trends. Logs are individual events – detailed, expensive, good for investigating.

**How do you scale Prometheus beyond one machine?** Shard scraping across many Prometheus servers and use a global query layer with object-storage blocks (Thanos, Cortex/Mimir).

**How do you avoid missed alerts if one evaluator dies?** Run two evaluators; the alert manager de-duplicates identical alerts.

## Wrap up

We collected labelled numbers into sharded, compressed time-series blocks, guarded cardinality, downsampled old data, and ran alert rules independently of dashboards.

> **📝 Key takeaways**
> - Count active series, not bytes; cardinality is the main risk.
> - Counters + `rate()`, histograms for percentiles.
> - Compressed, time-ordered blocks and downsampling keep storage cheap.
> - Alerts use a `for:` duration and must keep working during incidents.

## Going deeper (optional)

The detailed version separates three clocks – collection time, aggregation windows and rule evaluation – and shows how each adds delay before an alert fires.

[![Collection, aggregation and evaluation have separate timing semantics.](lessons/hld-17-flow.svg)](lessons/hld-17-flow.svg)

Further reading: [Prometheus documentation](https://prometheus.io/docs/introduction/overview/) and [Gorilla: A Fast, Scalable, In-Memory Time Series Database](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol8/p1816-teller.pdf).

## Closing answer

"Each service exposes counters, gauges and histograms with a small, fixed set of labels. Collectors scrape them every 10 seconds – batch jobs push through a gateway – and ingest enforces per-service series limits, because cardinality is the main danger. Samples are sharded by series into an in-memory head block with a write-ahead log, then compressed with delta and XOR encoding into 2-hour blocks in object storage, with downsampled rollups for long ranges. Queries fan out to shards and merge partial aggregates. Alert rules run every 30 seconds and fire only after their `for:` duration, through an alert manager that groups and routes pages, with a watchdog that checks monitoring itself."

topics.title: AI Observability & Evaluation
topics.concepts: Tracing, metrics, token usage, evaluation, hallucination detection
topics.markdown:
## Problem

Your HR assistant has been live for a month. A manager asks three questions you can't answer: "Is it getting better or worse?", "Why did it tell Asha the wrong leave balance on Tuesday?" and "Is it safe to switch to the cheaper model?"

LLM apps fail quietly – a fluent wrong answer looks just like a right one. **Observability** (seeing what happened on each request) and **evaluation** (measuring quality on known cases) are how you answer those questions.

## Requirements

- Trace every request: prompt, retrieval, tool calls, model, tokens, latency, cost.
- Build an evaluation set and score answers (correctness, faithfulness, relevance, safety).
- Use LLM-as-judge carefully, calibrated against humans.
- Gate releases (prompt, model or retrieval changes) on evaluation results.
- Use Spring AI's observability and evaluators.

## Step 1: The idea in plain words

| Practice | Question it answers | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Tracing** | "What exactly happened on this request?" | Every request, in production |
| **Metrics** | "How are latency, cost and errors trending?" | Continuously, on dashboards |
| **Offline evaluation** | "Is version B better than version A?" | Before every release |
| **Online feedback** | "Are real users satisfied?" | Thumbs up/down, escalations |

| Term | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Trace / span** | A record of one request and each step inside it (retrieval, model call, tool). |
| **Evaluation set** | Real questions with expected answers or sources, kept fixed and versioned. |
| **Faithfulness** | Every claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved sources. |
| **LLM-as-judge** | Using a model to score answers against a rubric. |
| **Release gate** | A rule like "no merge if correctness drops more than 2 points". |

> **🎯 In the interview**
> Interviewers usually ask: how you know your LLM app works; what you log; how you evaluate RAG; whether LLM-as-judge is reliable; how you compare models safely.

## Step 2: How evaluation and tracing fit together: the execution flow

[![Selected design: versioned test cases feed an evaluation runner, which calls the system under test; execution traces and scoring rubrics produce scores; human calibration checks the automatic judge; a release gate allows or blocks the change.](designs/ai-17.svg)](designs/ai-17.svg)

**In production, every request produces a trace:**

```text
trace 9f2c…  user=asha  route=/hr/ask  prompt=hr-answer-v7  model=gpt-4o-mini
├─ retrieval       42 ms   topK=4  sources=[Leave v4 §3.2, Leave v4 §3.3, …]
├─ chat model     1,380 ms tokens in=2,310 out=180  cost=₹0.06
└─ validation       3 ms   citations=2 ok
```

**Before a release, the evaluation runner:**

1. Runs all 200 cases in the evaluation set through the new version.
2. Scores each answer: correct? faithful to sources? relevant? safe?
3. Compares with the current version.
4. Passes or blocks the release.

Worked example – switching to a cheaper model:

```text
                       current (v7)   candidate (cheaper model)
Correctness              88%            86%
Faithfulness             95%            89%      ← dropped 6 points
"Not found" handled      92%            93%
Cost per answer          ₹0.06          ₹0.02
p95 latency              2.1 s          1.4 s
Gate: faithfulness must not drop > 2 points → BLOCK
```

![Animation: a candidate change runs through the evaluation set; correctness is close to the current version but faithfulness drops by six points; the release gate blocks it; after a prompt fix, faithfulness recovers and the gate passes.](learning-figures/ai-17-gate.gif)

> **⚖️ Design choice**
> Gate on the metrics that matter most for this product (here, faithfulness for HR answers), and look at cost and latency alongside – a cheaper model is only a win if quality holds.

## Step 3: In code with Spring AI

**Observability** – Spring AI emits Micrometer observations for ChatClient calls, advisors, model calls, tool calls and vector store queries. Add Actuator and a tracing bridge (OpenTelemetry), and you get spans and metrics such as `gen_ai.client.token.usage` and `gen_ai.client.operation`:

```properties
management.tracing.sampling.probability=1.0
management.otlp.tracing.endpoint=http://otel-collector:4318/v1/traces
# Prompt and completion content are NOT logged by default (privacy). Enable only in safe environments:
spring.ai.chat.client.observations.log-prompt=false
spring.ai.chat.observations.log-completion=false
```

**Evaluation** – Spring AI includes evaluators that use a model as a judge:

```java
@SpringBootTest
class HrAssistantEvaluationTest {
    @Autowired HrAssistant assistant;
    @Autowired ChatClient.Builder judgeBuilder;
    @Autowired VectorStore vectorStore;

    @ParameterizedTest
    @CsvFileSource(resources = "/eval/hr-questions-v3.csv", numLinesToSkip = 1)
    void answerIsRelevantAndGrounded(String question) {
        List<Document> sources = vectorStore.similaritySearch(question);
        String answer = assistant.ask(question);

        var request = new EvaluationRequest(question, sources, answer);
        assertTrue(new RelevancyEvaluator(judgeBuilder).evaluate(request).isPass(), "relevance");
        assertTrue(new FactCheckingEvaluator(judgeBuilder).evaluate(request).isPass(),
                "grounded in sources");
    }
}
```

- `RelevancyEvaluator` – does the answer address the question, given the context?
- `FactCheckingEvaluator` – is the answer supported by the provided documents?
- In practice, collect scores across all cases and compare aggregates rather than failing on one case.

## Step 4: Common mistakes

| Mistake | Better |
| --- | --- |
| "It looked fine in a few manual tries" | A fixed, versioned evaluation set of real questions |
| Only measuring the final answer | Also measure retrieval (recall@k) and tool success |
| Trusting an LLM judge blindly | Calibrate on 50–100 human-labelled cases; check agreement |
| Logging full prompts with personal data | Redact; restrict access; set retention |
| Averages only | Look at the worst cases and at safety-critical categories separately |
| Changing the eval set with every release | Version it; add cases, don't silently rewrite them |

> **⚠️ Common mistake**
> Letting average scores hide rare but serious failures. A 1% rate of leaking another employee's data is a disaster even if the overall score is 95%. Safety and security cases need their own zero-tolerance gate.

[![Security and rare high-impact cases need separate gates.](lessons/ai-17-failure.svg)](lessons/ai-17-failure.svg)

## Step 5: Production concerns

- **Sampling:** trace 100% of requests at first; sample later if volume is high, but keep all errors.
- **Cost dashboards:** tokens and cost per route, per user group and per model; alert on spikes.
- **Feedback loop:** thumbs-down answers and escalations become new evaluation cases.
- **Drift:** re-run the evaluation set on a schedule – providers update models, and your documents change.
- **Pin versions:** prompt version, model version and index version in every trace, so you can reproduce an answer.

## Interviewer follow-ups

**How do you evaluate a RAG system?** Separately: retrieval (did we fetch the right sources – recall@k) and generation (faithfulness, correctness, relevance), plus "not found" behaviour on questions outside the documents.

**Is LLM-as-judge reliable?** Reasonably, for clear rubrics, once you check it agrees with humans. Use a strong judge model, ask for a short reason, and avoid judging with the same model you're testing when possible.

**How do you debug one bad answer?** Find its trace: which prompt and model version, which chunks were retrieved, which tools ran. Usually the cause is visible there.

**How do you A/B test in production?** Route a small percentage of traffic to the new version, compare feedback, escalations, cost and latency, and keep offline evaluation as the first gate.

## Wrap up

Trace every request with versions, tokens and steps; measure quality on a fixed evaluation set; calibrate automatic judges with humans; and gate releases on the metrics that matter.

> **📝 Key takeaways**
> - Traces explain single answers; evaluation sets compare versions.
> - Score retrieval and generation separately.
> - Calibrate LLM judges against human labels.
> - Gate releases; give safety failures their own zero-tolerance gate.

## Going deeper (optional)

The detailed version versions inputs and scoring rubrics together so comparisons stay meaningful, and records human calibration results next to judge scores.

[![Versioned inputs and scoring rules make comparisons meaningful.](lessons/ai-17-flow.svg)](lessons/ai-17-flow.svg)

Further reading: [Spring AI – Observability](https://docs.spring.io/spring-ai/reference/observability/index.html) and [Spring AI – Evaluation testing](https://docs.spring.io/spring-ai/reference/api/testing.html).

## Closing answer

"LLM apps fail quietly, so I invest in observability and evaluation. Every request is traced with the prompt, model and index versions, retrieved sources, tool calls, tokens, cost and latency – Spring AI emits Micrometer observations that I export with OpenTelemetry, without logging personal data. Before any change – a prompt, a model or retrieval – I run a fixed, versioned evaluation set of real questions and score retrieval recall, correctness, faithfulness and relevance, using LLM-as-judge evaluators like Spring AI's relevancy and fact-checking evaluators, calibrated against human labels. A release gate blocks regressions, safety cases have zero tolerance, and user feedback keeps adding new cases."
